title: Support operations review: September
scratchpad:
sept tickets 1210?? merged dupes -> 1080
Tidepost live Nov 16
urgent = 2h to eng
macros: Callum, 90d
segments: Okay, let's get going, we've got a lot in the deck. This is the September support review. Felix, you and Lotte put this together?
Lotte did most of it, I mostly added opinions in the comments. One thing up front: the numbers stop at the end of September, so yesterday's scheduler mess isn't in here.
Good, that one's getting its own review anyway, so let's leave it out of this conversation completely. Lotte, take it away.
Thanks. Headline first. September came in at twelve hundred and ten tickets, which is up from nine hundred and seventy in August.
So that's roughly a twenty five percent jump month over month, and most of it landed in the last two weeks of the month.
That tracks with how it felt. The last two weeks it was like every customer discovered the recurring jobs feature on the same morning.
Recurring jobs is a big part of it, yeah, we'll get to categories in a second. Lotte, do first response before we get distracted.
Median first response time was four point two hours for the month. That's across all tickets, including everything that comes in overnight and on weekends.
Four point two hours feels high to me. What was it in August, roughly? I don't remember it being anywhere near that bad.
Three point one hours in August. So it did get worse, but the volume went up by a quarter and we had exactly the same team.
And honestly, the weekend tickets wreck the median. Anything that comes in Saturday morning sits until Monday, which is basically forty eight hours.
Do we have it split out by business hours? That's the number I actually care about when we set a target for next quarter.
I can pull it during the meeting, but the export from Burrowdesk is slow. Give me ten minutes or so and I'll have the business hours median.
On the target itself, my proposal for Q4 is a one hour median first response, business hours only. I think the team can get there.
One hour is tight, with everything else going on. If it's strictly business hours, though, maybe. I'd want to see the baseline first.
Let's hold the target until Lotte has the business hours number. There's no point setting a goal against the wrong baseline.
Okay, categories. Number one, by a distance, is scheduling conflicts. Double booked technicians, jobs landing on the wrong day, that kind of thing.
That's twenty eight percent of all tickets. And within that, more than half mention recurring jobs specifically, either in the subject or the first message.
The recurring jobs ones are almost all the same question. Someone edits one visit and expects the whole series to change, or the other way around.
So that's a product problem dressed up as a support problem. Has anyone actually sent this over to Jun's team yet?
I sent a summary last week, they know about it. The fix is a clearer prompt when you edit a recurring job. It's on their list.
Second is technician app login, at nineteen percent. Mostly password resets, and people stuck on an old version of the app that never updated.
We could kill half of those with a better macro, honestly. The current password reset macro still describes the old login screen, with the old buttons.
Third is invoices not syncing to accounting software, at fourteen percent. Fourth is notification emails landing in spam, at nine percent.
The invoice sync ones take the longest by far. Every single one is a little investigation, and they bounce back and forth between us and engineering.
Right, invoice sync tickets took three point five days on average to resolve, versus less than a day for everything else combined.
Three and a half days is a long time for someone waiting to get paid. I assume that feeds straight into the escalation conversation.
It does. Short version of my proposal: urgent tickets go to engineering after four hours without a fix, instead of the three days we have now. More on that later.
Okay, let's come back to that properly. Callum, do you want to take the macros and the knowledge base while we're on tooling?
Sure. So we have a hundred and sixty two macros right now. I went through the usage report, and about half of them haven't been used in two months.
Some reference features we've renamed, some reference the old pricing page, and a few are just duplicates with slightly different greetings at the top.
The duplicates are partly my fault. Everyone wrote their own version when they started, and nobody ever went back and cleaned up after them.
My proposal is to archive anything that hasn't been used in sixty days, and then rewrite the top twenty macros from scratch, properly this time.
I can take that on if Callum's swamped. I've got the usage export open anyway, and most of it is just a filtering job in a spreadsheet.
And the knowledge base? Customers keep telling me the help center search returns articles from two years ago, with screenshots that don't match anything.
The knowledge base is worse, honestly. Two hundred and twelve articles, and I'd guess forty of them are outdated or just flat out wrong.
The worst part is the screenshots. Half of them still show the old navigation from before the redesign, so people get lost following them.
We shouldn't touch the screenshots before we know what the help center looks like in the new tool, though. That's really the migration question.
Right, let's do the migration then, since everything seems to depend on it. Lotte, where are we with moving off Burrowdesk?
The Tidepost contract is signed, the sandbox is set up, and we've mapped about eighty percent of the fields from Burrowdesk so far.
The plan we had was to cut over on Monday the second of November. Run both tools in parallel for a week, then switch Burrowdesk off.
If we cut over on the second, we'd be migrating a hundred and sixty two macros, half of which I'm about to delete. That seems backwards to me.
Agreed, the cleanup should happen before the move, not after it. Otherwise we're spending time carefully moving junk into a brand new tool.
There's another problem, too. Burrowdesk throttles their export API, and we have six years of attachments in there. The full export is slow.
How slow are we talking? Days or weeks? Because that changes the shape of the whole plan pretty fundamentally.
I ran a test export of a single month last night. It took about seven hours. So the whole archive is more than a week, maybe ten days.
Do we even need six years of attachments in the new tool? Nobody is looking at a photo of a broken boiler from twenty twenty.
Legally we need two years searchable. The rest can go to cold storage as an archive file. That cuts the export down a lot.
Okay, so before anything moves, I'd want the macro cleanup done, and Lotte does the slimmer export. When does that actually land us?
Realistically, two weeks later than the plan. So Tidepost goes live on Monday the sixteenth of November, with Burrowdesk read-only for a week after.
Okay, I'm fine with the sixteenth. I'd rather have a clean cutover than a fast one. Felix, does that work with the shift schedule?
It works. It also means the launch rush happens entirely on Burrowdesk, which everyone already knows inside out. That's honestly a relief.
So the macro cleanup is the thing gating the migration. Who owns it, and by when? Lotte, you offered earlier.
I did, but with the export work on top, I don't think I can do both well. The export is going to eat my next two weeks.
I'll take it. I know the macros better than anyone anyway, I wrote half of the bad ones myself, so it's only fair.
And I'd change my own rule. Sixty days is too aggressive, some macros are seasonal, like the holiday scheduling ones. Let's say ninety days instead.
Ninety is better. The holiday ones only get used in December, and I really don't want to rewrite them from scratch every year.
So, final answer, I'll archive every macro unused for ninety days and rewrite the top twenty, all done by Friday the twenty-third of October.
Perfect, that leaves a few weeks of buffer before the cutover. And the knowledge base, does that move before or after?
The knowledge base I'd fix in Tidepost directly, after the cutover. There's no point fixing screenshots in a tool we're about to leave.
Agreed. The knowledge base cleanup is a December project. Let's not pretend we're going to squeeze it into November with everything else.
Oh, by the way, I've got the business hours number now. The export finally finished while we were talking about macros.
Business hours only, the September median first response was two point six hours. So the weekends were inflating it quite a lot.
Two point six. That's still not great, but it's a very different story from four point two. Okay, that's useful.
Which makes my one hour target look a bit silly. Going from two point six to one in a single quarter, with a migration in the middle, isn't happening.
And we always lose a few days of speed around any cutover. Everyone's learning a new tool, new shortcuts, new everything.
Let me revise it, then. The Q4 target is a ninety minute median first response, business hours. That's ambitious, but I think we can hit it.
Ninety minutes, business hours, median. I'm good with that. Let's report it weekly, though, not just at the end of the month.
I'll add it to the Monday report. I'll show the all hours number next to it too, so we don't lose sight of the weekends.
Actually, while I had that export open I found a problem with my headline number, so I owe everyone a correction.
The twelve hundred and ten double counts merged tickets. When a customer emails twice and we merge the threads, Burrowdesk counts both of them.
Of course it does. That tool, honestly. How much does that change the picture? Are we talking a rounding error or a real difference?
A real difference. After taking out merged duplicates and the spam that got through the filter, September was a thousand and eighty tickets.
So a thousand and eighty, compared to what for August? Is August inflated the same way, or was it cleaner?
August had fewer merges, so it drops less. Clean August is about nine hundred and twenty. So the real growth is closer to seventeen percent.
That's a relief, honestly. Seventeen percent I can plan around. Twenty five percent was starting to make me nervous about the next quarter.
Lotte, please fix the deck before it goes anywhere else, and add a footnote about the merge counting so nobody repeats the mistake.
Okay, escalation. I floated four hours for urgent tickets earlier. I talked to Jun about it on Tuesday, before everything caught fire yesterday.
His view is that four hours is too long for the really bad ones. If a customer can't dispatch at all, engineering wants to know almost immediately.
But we also can't pull engineering in every time someone can't find a button. The urgent label already gets abused, constantly.
Last month we tagged forty one tickets as urgent, and when I reread them all, maybe twelve were actually urgent by any sane definition.
So the label needs a real definition first, and then the clock can be shorter. Felix, what's the definition you'd use?
Urgent means a customer can't dispatch jobs, technicians can't log in at all, or invoices are failing for every customer. Nothing else counts.
With that definition, I'd go shorter than four hours. Let's say urgent tickets escalate to engineering after two hours without a fix. Everything else stays at three days.
Two hours with a strict definition, yes. I'd much rather escalate a few real ones early than a lot of fake ones late.
Who decides what's urgent, though? If it's whoever happens to pick up the ticket, we're right back to forty one a month.
The senior person on shift decides. Callum or me during the week, and whoever's on the weekend rotation on Saturdays and Sundays.
Good. Felix, can you write the definition into the escalation doc and send it to Jun's team, so nobody over there is surprised?
Yes, I'll write it up and have it over to Jun's team by Monday, along with the two hour rule and who makes the call.
Which brings us to the schedule. Felix, what's the weekend plan? Right now Sunday coverage is basically nobody checking the queue.
Right. Starting Saturday the seventeenth of October, we rotate weekend coverage. One person each day, four hour shifts, rotating across the specialists.
Do people get a weekday off in exchange? Otherwise that's going to go down badly with the team, and very quickly.
Yes, a weekday off the following week, their choice. I've already run it past everyone informally, and nobody screamed, which is a good sign.
And the early shift? Some customers start their day at six and keep opening tickets before any of us are online.
The early shift moves to seven in the morning, starting the same week. Callum volunteered for it, which I'm going to hold him to.
I did volunteer. I'm an early person anyway, and I'd rather finish at three and actually see some daylight.
Good. Felix, when does the written schedule go out to the team? People need some notice to plan their lives around it.
I'll publish it by next Friday, the ninth, so everyone has a full week's notice before the first weekend shift.
Great. Anything else before we wrap up? I want to make sure the cutover risk is clearly on someone's plate, not just floating around.
I'll own the cutover checklist. The parallel run, the read-only week, and a rollback plan in case Tidepost falls over on the first day.
One more thing. The September numbers go into the monthly update. Can we please use the corrected thousand and eighty, not the old number?
Yes, corrected numbers only, everywhere. Okay, thanks everyone, this was really useful. Lotte, send the fixed deck around when it's ready.

items.text: September volume was 1,080 tickets after removing merged duplicates and spam (first reported as 1,210)
Tidepost cutover moves to Monday, November 16; Burrowdesk stays read-only for a week after
Urgent tickets escalate to engineering after two hours without a fix; everything else stays at three days
Q4 target: a ninety-minute median first response in business hours
Archive macros unused for ninety days and rewrite the top twenty by Friday, October 23
Write the urgent definition into the escalation doc and send it to Jun's team by Monday
Publish the weekend rotation schedule by Friday the 9th
Own the Tidepost cutover checklist, including a rollback plan
